articles.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.
articles.content:
An international research team has identified seven previously undescribed species of Madagascar's elusive diamond frogs (Rhombophryne), adding new evidence that this unusual amphibian group is far more diverse than scientists once realized.

Accurately identifying species and understanding where they live are essential for measuring biodiversity and protecting it. To sort out the identities of these frogs, researchers combined field observations, museum specimens, and advanced DNA analysis. The work revealed previously hidden species diversity and helped resolve a taxonomic problem that had remained unsettled for years.

By determining which frogs belong to which species and mapping where they occur, the researchers have also created a stronger scientific basis for conservation in Madagascar, where many forests are rapidly disappearing.

"Diamond frogs have been hiding their diversity beneath our feet," said Dr. Mark D. Scherz, Curator of Herpetology at the Natural History Museum Denmark and lead author of the study.

"Many species spend most of their lives beneath the leaf litter, and even when they emerge they can look deceptively similar," he added.

Madagascar's Secretive Diamond Frogs

Diamond frogs are some of Madagascar's most distinctive amphibians. Certain species are extremely round and resemble the rain frogs found in mainland Africa, spending much of their time concealed beneath the forest floor. Other species have long legs and live among moss, while some are sturdier frogs adapted to life on the ground.

Most diamond frogs look brown at first, but several species have vivid markings that remain hidden until the frogs move. These can include bright orange flashes or bold white and black patterns on the thighs and lower back. Researchers think these markings may help startle predators.

Because these frogs are so difficult to find and observe, diamond frogs remain among the least studied vertebrates in Madagascar.

A 12 Year Scientific Puzzle

The research effort began more than twelve years ago, when scientists repeatedly encountered frogs that clearly appeared to represent species that had never been formally described. Identifying them was not simple, however, because researchers had trouble matching older species names with the genetic lineages found in modern specimens.

"When I started this project twelve years ago, we already knew there were several species waiting to be described, and almost every expedition to Madagascar revealed another one. Some were relatively straightforward to describe, but others were complicated by uncertainty surrounding older species names. Untangling that puzzle took years," Scherz said.

A major breakthrough came from museomics, the use of DNA sequencing on historical museum specimens. Researchers compared genetic information from old collections with DNA from newly collected frogs. They also examined external features, skeletal anatomy, and frog calls.

Together, those lines of evidence allowed the team to connect historical species names with the correct evolutionary lineages and clear up taxonomic confusion that had persisted for decades.

Museum collections played a central role in establishing the identities of several of the species.

"Museum collections are far more than archives of the past - they are essential scientific resources for understanding biodiversity today," said Dr. Alice Petzold of the University of Potsdam, who led the museomics work.

"By sequencing historical specimens, including the original type specimens, we were able to answer questions that have persisted for generations," she added.

New Species Could Shape Conservation

The study was carried out through close cooperation among scientists and institutions in Madagascar and Europe. It also highlights the direct connection between biodiversity research and conservation.

Many diamond frogs live in forests that are becoming increasingly fragmented by deforestation. At the same time, scientists still know very little about the basic biology of many of these species.

"For many species, we still know almost nothing about their breeding biology, population sizes or ecological requirements. Without that knowledge, it becomes much more difficult to assess their conservation status and protect them effectively," said co-author Dr. Andolalao Rakotoarison of the Institut d'Enseignement Supérieur de Soavinandriana Itasy, Madagascar.

The new findings are already contributing to conservation planning in Madagascar. At a protected area planning workshop held in March 2026 as part of the country's Biodiversity 30x30Program, several of the newly described frogs, including Rhombophryne quentini, directly informed proposals aimed at strengthening and expanding protected areas.

More Frogs May Still Be Waiting

With the addition of seven new species, the number of known Rhombophryne species has risen to 27. Even so, the researchers believe more unnamed species are almost certain to remain undiscovered and undescribed.

The new study resolves many long-standing questions, but Scherz views it as the start of a much larger effort.

"Every newly described species represents millions of years of unique evolutionary history. The more we learn about Madagascar's remarkable amphibians, the clearer it becomes that there is still an enormous amount left to discover," he said.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the discovery of seven new frog species in Madagascar using advanced DNA techniques, which significantly enhances understanding of biodiversity. This has broad implications for conservation efforts in a region facing rapid habitat loss, providing a strong scientific basis to protect these species and their environment. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights meaningful progress in biodiversity research and conservation planning.

articles.title: Manhattan’s flood walls are almost done. What will Mamdani do next?
articles.content:
New York City has more than 500 miles of coastline. The city’s coastal zone is home to more than 1 million people as well as billions of dollars of residential and commercial property, and no two miles of the waterfront are quite the same. The marshy areas of southern Queens, the housing projects in waterfront Brooklyn, and the towers of Manhattan’s Financial District are all vulnerable during high tides and major storm events, and each of these areas is vulnerable in a different way.

The city learned these lessons the hard way in 2012 when Superstorm Sandy sent almost 14 feet of storm surge up New York Harbor and flooded thousands of structures across the five boroughs. In the aftermath of the disaster, the city embarked on one of the most ambitious climate adaptation efforts in U.S. history. Leaders spent billions of dollars to elevate and armor the lower reaches of Manhattan with flood gates and berms, rebuild the destroyed beaches in Queens, and buy out homes in the low-lying neighborhoods of Staten Island.

Each stage of this effort faced delay and controversy, but the post-Sandy effort is now almost complete. The elevated East River Park in Manhattan is now partly open to sunbathers and tennis players. Farther down the island, construction crews are installing rolling-track flood walls that will be deployed during major storm surge events. These flood defenses will be operational by the 2027 hurricane season, but Mayor Zohran Mamdani is already laying the groundwork for what comes next.

Last month the mayor announced a major expansion of the Bureau of Coastal Resilience, promising to add almost 70 new staff members to a unit that had been on a shoestring budget under prior mayor Eric Adams. The first members of this new team will deploy the flood gates and clear the coastal zone in the runup to big storm events.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“There was this huge investment of over a billion dollars to build these gates, and once you build it, you have to maintain it,” said Lisa Garcia, the new commissioner for the Department of Environmental Protection, which will oversee the flood system. (Garcia was the director of Grist’s climate solutions lab from 2019 to 2021, and later worked as a regional director in the Environmental Protection Agency.)

But managing the gates is the easy part. The harder task for Mamdani will be to decide what the city’s next big flood protection effort should be. The stakes of this decision are higher than almost anywhere else in the United States, or for any other climate adaptation in New York. While heat waves, smoke, and flash floods all pose big risks to the city, sea level rise and storm surge have the potential to wipe out huge sections of the city’s most populous areas and cripple its economy.

“I don’t think that there’s anyone who is saying we can protect all 520 miles of coastline,” said Garcia. “So part of it is this… What lessons can we take to other boroughs or to other communities?”

Mamdani will have to make some big decisions about where and how to spend the city’s limited capital budget. Is it better to fund marsh restoration in outer Queens, or a coastal park in Harlem, or a bulkhead in the waterfront of Brooklyn? If you want to do all of those things, which of them do you do first?

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

These decisions are fraught with political and economic risks. When Norfolk, Virginia, another coastal city, created its master resilience plan, city officials made the controversial decision not to build flood protections for areas that were at high risk of flooding but didn’t have the high-value property that would justify the enormous expense. Under its plan, Norfolk would instead help those residents of the “yellow zones” live with rising waters or relocate elsewhere. In other coastal areas like California and North Carolina, efforts to promote “managed retreat” from vulnerable areas have met forceful blowback from residents who want structural protections.

For its part, New York City says it’s still in the early phases of planning for future protections. Mamdani won the mayoral election last year by assembling a coalition that spanned all the lower-income neighborhoods of the outer boroughs, and he took office promising to make life more affordable for the city’s lower and middle classes. The Department of Environmental Protection said it plans to start its master plan (which Garcia wants to analyze both stormwater flooding and coastal risk) next year, with a goal of finishing by 2031. It’s too early, then, to say how Mamdani’s governing philosophy will affect the city’s approach to the risks of climate change.

There is no shortage of underserved areas that need flood protection. But perhaps the most glaring example is the western edge of Coney Island, which faces routine “backdoor” flooding during heavy rain as the ocean rushes up through creeks and out of the drainage system. This flooding often makes it impossible for children to walk to school. Even though Coney Island was one of the neighborhoods hit hardest by Sandy in 2012, the city still hasn’t built new flood defenses there.

“After Sandy, neighborhoods in Manhattan had millions and millions of dollars invested,” said Pamela Pettyjohn, the founder of the Coney Island Beautification Project, a neighborhood group that advocates for flood protection and quality-of-life improvements. “There hasn’t been any investment at all in Coney Island other than development — a lot of new development, new buildings, but nothing for the infrastructure.” The city government is now holding meetings with Coney Island residents to decide how to reduce flood risk along local creeks.

In other areas, architects and planners have sketched out possible defenses for which there is no available money. In East Harlem, for instance, the city worked with architecture firm One Architecture to design a plan that would drain stormwater that pools in low-lying streets and elevate the esplanades along the river. The plan has been around for almost a decade, but the city has not been able to raise any money for it. In other cases, flood defense efforts have fallen through due to budget constraints: The city pivoted its proposed flood adaptation project in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the Bronx to a cheaper project that will provide off-grid backup power to the area’s critical food depot.

“We can plan for it, but it’s all about priorities,” said Amy Chester, the director of Rebuild by Design, the organization that led the post-Sandy adaptation effort.

The other problem is that people often disagree about how a given area should defend against flooding, and about what counts as sufficient investment. Garcia has said that in some cases a flood gate or bulwark may be the best scenario, while in other cases home buyouts or nature-based living shorelines may work better.

City officials have already encountered pushback over at least one of its projects. The city broke ground late last year on a project in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Red Hook, which was also hit hard by Sandy. The effort will elevate streets and install new bulkheads along the water, but residents and activists say it’s inadequate: it is only designed to protect against “10-year storms” that have a 1-in-10 chance of happening in a given year, not the much larger “100-year storms” that the Lower Manhattan projects will protect against.

The issue of flood risk has also come up farther north in the gentrified neighborhood of Greenpoint. In that area, a real estate developer is proposing to build a large new apartment complex that will contain more than 1,300 homes. The new towers will have steel bulkheads that the developer says will protect them from flooding, but some activists have protested that the bulkhead will push water onto nearby areas.

These two controversies highlight the extent to which the city’s current flood defenses are a patchwork of individual neighborhood projects. That approach will lead to conflict over each investment and over where the city chooses to invest, says Matthijs Bouw, an architect with the firm One Architecture who helped conceive the flood barrier project that now surrounds lower Manhattan and who has also envisioned flood protections in East Harlem and other areas.

“You can’t build this stuff in isolation, you need to find a way to make sure that you align whatever you design with the way the city changes over time,” he said.

In theory, planners could come up with a comprehensive process for deciding where and how to spend its money, but there are tough choices involved in such a process. Lower Manhattan was an easy place to start after Sandy, since it was home to both the all-important cluster of downtown skyscrapers and a dense neighborhood of vulnerable public housing, but figuring out where to go next is harder.

articles.title: ‘The lake is our life’: Protecting a shared lifeline in Uganda
articles.summary: On the shores of Nkondo, in Uganda’s Kikuube district, the day begins before sunrise. Fishers enter the lake to fish, while families around Lake Albert rely on its waters for food, income and daily survival.
articles.content:
But, behind these daily activities lies an increasingly visible threat: plastic waste and other debris entering Lake Albert.

Leaders of the local fishing community are warning that without urgent action, pollution could endanger fish stocks and, as a consequence, the lives of future generations.

Like the local fishers, the UN has also warned of the decline of freshwater species due to pollution and environmental degradation in recent decades.

Surface water bodies are shrinking or being completely lost in areas home to 93.1 million people, while more than a quarter are becoming increasingly cloudy because of pollution, according to a 2024 report by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and UN-Water.

In celebration of World Lake Day, marked annually on 27 August, Solomon Wamara, the chairperson for fishers on Lake Albert, said the community cannot continue to view the lake as a source of livelihood while allowing it to be filled with waste.

“It is a good time to highlight the threats facing this lake that is our lifeline,” he told UN News.

Plastics threaten fish breeding grounds

For Mr. Wamara, plastic waste is not just a sanitation issue. It directly affects the future of fishing and food security.

He said that when plastic bags and other waste are thrown away, they eventually end up in the lake, where they can affect the areas where fish breed and grow.

But the pollution doesn’t stop at the lake’s shores.

Agricultural activities and waste disposal often carry waste from the Wambaya, Waki and Nguse rivers into Lake Albert, Mr. Wamara said.

“River pollution affects fish breeding grounds and also food security. These rivers are essential for the survival of fish and communities that depend on the lake,” he said. “The lake is our life.”

Society’s responsibility

The community should change the way it cares for the lake, according to Mr. Wamara.

He urged communities living around Lake Albert to stop dumping waste – especially plastic – and to participate in environmental sanitation activities.

Mr. Wamara supports monthly the cleanliness campaigns and say such efforts should be expanded and involve more communities.

Conservation efforts should also consider the financial situation of the people whose livelihoods depend on the lake, he said.

Rather than excessively taxing traditional fishers, he said authorities should help them continue fishing sustainably and within the law.

UN News

A common resource

Godwin Angalia, the Kikuube district commissioner, who also comes from a fishing community and was once a fisher, said the government sees lakes as an important pillar of local economies and people’s lives.

“As a government, we value lakes because they enable the lives of millions of citizens,” Mr. Angalia said. “They also provide various resources that support society."

However, Lake Albert faces several challenges, including environmental pollution and illegal fishing.

According to Mr. Angalia, the government continues to take steps to combat pollution resulting from human activities while also aiming to protect the water sources that feed the lake.

“Of course, rivers like Nguse and Wambaya have been polluted,” he said. “Also, the Bugoma Forest is very important for the life of Lake Albert and the creatures in it.”

Mr. Angalia said efforts are ongoing to protect the Bugoma Forest and the rivers that empty their waters into Lake Albert from destruction and pollution.

He has also urged village leaders to be vigilant and report people who pollute the environment or destroy lake resources to the relevant authorities.

UN News

Fishers’ role

In addition to government measures, Mr. Angalia said the community should be part of the solution.

The government has begun forming indigenous community committees that will assist in fisheries management in their areas.

Mr. Angalia said fishers’ participation is important because they are familiar with the lake’s environment and understand how its resources can be used without depleting them.

“We fishermen ourselves know that we should not catch young fish,” he said. “We use natural and environmentally friendly methods in fishing.”

For Mr. Angalia, fishers are at the center of discussions around conservation, not only as part of the problem, but also as important guardians of the resources they depend on.

Future in everyone’s hands

As human activity increases, so does the pressure on Lake Albert’s ecosystem.

For surrounding residents, the message is clear: the lake cannot be protected by the government alone.

If Lake Albert is to continue sustaining the food, income and livelihoods of communities like Mr. Wamara’s, protecting it isn’t an option, but a necessity.

“If we protect the lake, we protect our lives and the lives of future generations,” he said.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le lac Albert en Ouganda est une source essentielle de nourriture et de revenus pour des millions de personnes vivant à proximité. Les pêcheurs et les familles dépendent du lac chaque jour, mais la pollution causée par les déchets plastiques et l’agriculture menace sa santé.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les pêcheurs locaux et les dirigeants gouvernementaux du district de Kikuube en Ouganda travaillent ensemble pour arrêter la pollution dans le lac Albert. Ils sensibilisent à l’impact des déchets plastiques sur les zones de reproduction des poissons et encouragent les communautés à ne plus jeter leurs déchets. Le gouvernement protège les rivières et forêts qui alimentent le lac et forme des comités locaux pour mieux gérer la pêche durablement.

**Impact** – Cet effort commun est important car la pollution pourrait réduire le nombre de poissons, mettant en danger l’alimentation et les emplois de nombreuses personnes. En impliquant les pêcheurs qui connaissent bien le lac, la communauté peut mieux protéger l’environnement tout en continuant à vivre de la pêche. Ces actions aident à garder le lac en bonne santé aujourd’hui et pour les générations futures.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement prévoit de continuer à protéger les rivières et forêts et d’élargir les campagnes de nettoyage. Les chefs locaux surveilleront la pollution et la pêche illégale. Les pêcheurs joueront un rôle plus important dans la gestion des ressources pour assurer une pêche durable et équitable.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – En Ouganda, les communautés et le gouvernement travaillent ensemble pour réduire la pollution du lac Albert, protégeant les stocks de poissons et les moyens de subsistance d’aujourd’hui et de demain.
articles.personality_title_es: Comunidad y gobierno de Uganda se unen para combatir la contaminación del lago Alberto
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El lago Alberto en Uganda es una fuente vital de alimento e ingresos para millones de personas que viven cerca. Los pescadores y familias dependen del lago cada día, pero la contaminación por desechos plásticos y la agricultura amenaza su salud.

**Qué pasó** – Los pescadores locales y líderes del gobierno en el distrito de Kikuube en Uganda están trabajando juntos para detener la contaminación en el lago Alberto. Están creando conciencia sobre los residuos plásticos que dañan las zonas donde los peces se reproducen y animando a las comunidades a dejar de tirar basura. El gobierno protege los ríos y bosques que alimentan el lago y forma comités locales para manejar la pesca de forma sostenible.

**Impacto** – Este esfuerzo conjunto es importante porque la contaminación podría reducir la cantidad de peces, poniendo en riesgo la comida y los empleos de muchas personas. Al involucrar a los pescadores que conocen bien el lago, la comunidad puede proteger mejor el medio ambiente mientras sigue ganándose la vida. Estas acciones ayudan a mantener el lago saludable ahora y para las futuras generaciones.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno planea continuar protegiendo los ríos y bosques y ampliar las campañas de limpieza. Los líderes locales vigilarán la contaminación y la pesca ilegal. Los pescadores tendrán un papel más importante en la gestión de los recursos para mantener la pesca sostenible y justa.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Comunidades y gobierno en Uganda trabajan juntos para reducir la contaminación del lago Alberto, protegiendo las poblaciones de peces y los medios de vida presentes y futuros.

articles.title: Nature reserves spot rare species during heatwaves
articles.summary: A wildlife trust says unusually hot weather and increased monitoring has led to interesting finds.
articles.content:
A wildlife trust said some species had been spotted in nature reserves this summer for the first time in years.

Volunteers for the Herts and Middlesex Wildlife Trust recorded a great white egret near Ware and more than 300 Chalkhill blue butterflies at Hexton Chalk Pit near Hitchin, where they also found a glow-worm for the first time in 25 years.

The trust said it was partly due to the unusually hot weather but also the result of increased surveying and monitoring in the county.

Senior reserves officer Dan Townsend said: "This summer we've had some extraordinary records, from species that haven't been recorded in Hertfordshire for decades to new discoveries for individual reserves."
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the positive discovery of rare species in nature reserves, indicating successful conservation efforts and increased biodiversity monitoring, which benefits the environment and public awareness.
articles.personality_title: Rare species spotted in nature reserves during hot summer
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – This summer, parts of England experienced unusually hot weather. At the same time, wildlife experts increased their efforts to watch and record animals and insects in nature reserves.

**What happened** – Volunteers from the Herts and Middlesex Wildlife Trust found several rare species in local nature reserves. They saw a great white egret near Ware, more than 300 Chalkhill blue butterflies at Hexton Chalk Pit near Hitchin, and a glow-worm in the same area for the first time in 25 years.

**Impact** – These discoveries show that some rare animals are returning or becoming easier to find. It suggests that the work to protect these places and study wildlife is working well. Finding a glow-worm after such a long time is especially important because it shows the environment can support sensitive species again.

**What's next step** – The wildlife trust will continue to monitor species closely to learn more about how animals respond to changing weather and conservation efforts. This will help them protect rare species and their homes better in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Hot weather and careful monitoring helped experts spot rare species returning to nature reserves after many years.
articles.personality_title_fr: Espèces rares observées dans les réserves naturelles pendant l'été chaud
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Cet été, certaines régions d'Angleterre ont connu un temps exceptionnellement chaud. En même temps, des experts en faune ont intensifié leurs efforts pour observer et enregistrer les animaux et insectes dans les réserves naturelles.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des volontaires du Herts and Middlesex Wildlife Trust ont découvert plusieurs espèces rares dans des réserves locales. Ils ont vu un grand héron blanc près de Ware, plus de 300 papillons bleu Chalkhill à Hexton Chalk Pit près de Hitchin, et une ver luisante dans cette même zone pour la première fois depuis 25 ans.

**Impact** – Ces découvertes montrent que certaines espèces rares reviennent ou deviennent plus faciles à trouver. Cela suggère que les efforts pour protéger ces lieux et étudier la faune fonctionnent bien. Trouver une ver luisante après tant d'années est particulièrement important, car cela montre que l'environnement peut de nouveau soutenir des espèces sensibles.

**Prochaine étape** – Le trust continuera à surveiller les espèces de près pour mieux comprendre comment les animaux réagissent aux changements climatiques et aux efforts de conservation. Cela les aidera à mieux protéger les espèces rares et leurs habitats à l'avenir.

**En résumé** – La chaleur estivale et une surveillance attentive ont aidé les experts à repérer des espèces rares revenant dans les réserves naturelles après de nombreuses années.
articles.personality_title_es: Especies raras avistadas en reservas naturales durante el verano caluroso
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Este verano, algunas partes de Inglaterra tuvieron un clima inusualmente caluroso. Al mismo tiempo, expertos en vida silvestre aumentaron sus esfuerzos para observar y registrar animales e insectos en reservas naturales.

**Qué pasó** – Voluntarios del Herts and Middlesex Wildlife Trust encontraron varias especies raras en reservas locales. Vieron una garza blanca cerca de Ware, más de 300 mariposas Chalkhill azul en Hexton Chalk Pit cerca de Hitchin, y una luciérnaga en la misma zona por primera vez en 25 años.

**Impacto** – Estos hallazgos muestran que algunas especies raras están regresando o son más fáciles de encontrar. Esto indica que el trabajo para proteger estos lugares y estudiar la vida silvestre está dando resultados. Encontrar una luciérnaga después de tantos años es especialmente importante porque muestra que el ambiente puede volver a sostener especies sensibles.

**Próximo paso** – El trust continuará monitoreando las especies de cerca para aprender más sobre cómo responden los animales al clima cambiante y a los esfuerzos de conservación. Esto les ayudará a proteger mejor las especies raras y sus hogares en el futuro.

**Resumen en una frase** – El clima cálido y la vigilancia cuidadosa ayudaron a los expertos a descubrir especies raras que regresan a las reservas naturales después de muchos años.
